latent_mechanisms.display_name: Chigger-bite inoculation with local Orientia replication
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Orientia tsutsugamushi is introduced by trombiculid mite larva bite, replicates in local dendritic cells/macrophages and endothelial cells, and produces a necrotic papule-eschar at the inoculation site when the local lesion is visible.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Orientia bloodstream dissemination and endothelial infection
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Intracellular Orientia disseminates via blood and lymphatics to vascular endothelium and mononuclear phagocytes in skin, lung, liver, kidney, heart, brain, and gastrointestinal tract. This pathogen-burden mechanism is the direct target of active anti-rickettsial antibiotics.
Endothelial and monocyte infection activates IL-6, TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, and acute-phase pathways, producing high fever, chills, headache, myalgia, malaise, CRP rise, and variable leukocyte response.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Systemic endothelial injury and small-vessel vasculitis
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Orientia tropism for endothelium produces vasculitis, perivasculitis, vascular leak, platelet consumption, D-dimer elevation, rash, lymphadenopathy, edema, and the shared substrate for organ complications.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Pulmonary interstitial pneumonitis and ARDS pathway
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Pulmonary endothelial infection and capillary leak cause interstitial pneumonitis, pleural effusion, hypoxemia, and in severe delayed cases diffuse infiltrates meeting ARDS physiology.

Hepatic sinusoidal endothelial infection and inflammatory cholestasis produce transaminitis, alkaline phosphatase rise, direct-predominant hyperbilirubinemia, hypoalbuminemia, hepatomegaly, and jaundice in severe disease.

Systemic endothelial activation consumes platelets and may trigger DIC in severe disease, producing thrombocytopenia, D-dimer elevation, PT/aPTT prolongation, bleeding risk, and microvascular ischemic events.
Renal small-vessel injury, interstitial inflammation, hypoperfusion, and occasional rhabdomyolysis or DIC overlap raise creatinine and BUN; severe disease can require renal replacement therapy.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Central nervous system vasculitis and meningoencephalitis
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Endothelial infection and inflammatory vasculitis in meninges and brain produce headache, meningismus, aseptic meningitis, encephalopathy, seizures, cranial neuropathies, cerebellitis, and rarely stroke or hemorrhage.
Myocardial endothelial and myocyte inflammation, plus cytokine-mediated vasodilation and capillary leak, can cause myocarditis, conduction abnormalities, hypotension, lactate rise, and shock.

Small-vessel vasculitis and capillary leak in gut, liver-spleen axis, and pancreas produce nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, ileus, ascites, GI bleeding, pancreatitis, and rare splenic infarction.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Local inoculation precedes hematogenous and lymphatic dissemination after the incubation period.
The black necrotic eschar is the local inoculation lesion; it may be hidden in axilla, groin, ear canal, scalp, or skin folds.
Visible eschars are usually small centimeter-scale crusted ulcers with surrounding erythematous halo.
Intracellular bacterial burden activates monocyte and endothelial cytokine pathways.

IL-6-driven acute-phase response elevates CRP, often into bacterial-infection ranges.

Fever and CRP share the cytokine-response mechanism.

Diffuse bilateral infiltrates indicate pulmonary capillary leak and ARDS physiology.
AST and ALT rise together in rickettsial hepatitis, though AST can be higher with muscle or ischemic injury.
Direct bilirubin and ALP track cholestatic hepatic injury.
Creatinine rise is the measured axis defining AKI severity.
Pancreatic enzyme elevation supports active pancreatitis.
Lipase is more specific than amylase for pancreatic injury.
Falling MAP is the bedside expression of shock transition.
ARDS is one of the main fatal complication paths.
Shock accelerates death risk through hypoperfusion, lactate rise, and multi-organ failure.
DIC increases mortality through hemorrhage, thrombosis, and organ failure.

recent_bush_grass_field_jungle_or_farm_e.trajectory_modulation: Raises prior for chigger-bite exposure; outdoor work, farming, military training, trekking, and rural travel are high-yield contexts.

local_high_incidence_season.trajectory_modulation: Clusters after rainy season, harvest, or autumn in many endemic regions.

visible_eschar_found.trajectory_modulation: Strong bedside clue and can reduce diagnostic delay.

no_eschar_found_after_full_skin_exam.trajectory_modulation: Absence lowers specificity but does not exclude scrub typhus.

hidden_site_not_examined.trajectory_modulation: Raises miss risk because eschars can be in axilla, groin, scalp, skin folds, or external auditory canal.

active_antibiotic_after_day_7.trajectory_modulation: More advanced endothelial injury; higher ARDS, AKI, DIC, myocarditis, CNS involvement, and mortality hazards.

active_antibiotic_within_first_week.trajectory_modulation: Faster fever clearance and lower organ-complication hazard.

age_over_60_or_major_comorbidity.trajectory_modulation: Higher complication and mortality hazard for the same pathogen/endothelial burden.

pregnant.trajectory_modulation: Higher fetal risk and modified antibiotic selection; avoid diagnostic delay.

platelets_below_100_or_albumin_below_3.trajectory_modulation: Amplifies ARDS, bleeding/DIC, AKI, and mortality hazards because it reflects systemic endothelial leak.

supportive_care: Perform full skin examination including axillae, groin, scalp, skin folds, and external auditory canal when scrub typhus is plausible.
Do not wait for serology or PCR before starting active anti-rickettsial therapy when clinical suspicion is high.
Record symptom-onset day and prior inactive antibiotic exposure, because delayed active therapy predicts organ complications.
Monitor fever curve, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, urine output, mental status, rash/eschar evolution, and abdominal pain at least daily in admitted patients.
Trend CBC with platelet count, AST/ALT, bilirubin fractions, ALP, albumin, creatinine, BUN, sodium, CRP, coagulation tests, and D-dimer in moderate or severe disease.
Escalate early for rising respiratory rate, falling oxygen saturation, or bilateral infiltrates; use lung-protective ventilation if ARDS develops.
Use balanced fluids cautiously in capillary leak; add vasopressors rather than pushing excessive crystalloid when oxygenation worsens.
Evaluate severe abdominal pain with pancreatic enzymes and abdominal imaging; pancreatitis care must be paired with active anti-Orientia therapy.
Assess CNS signs including meningismus, altered mental status, seizures, cranial neuropathy, and cerebellar signs; avoid unsafe lumbar puncture when raised ICP or coagulopathy is present.
Avoid assuming beta-lactam clinical nonresponse excludes infection; beta-lactams do not reliably treat intracellular Orientia.
Manage DIC or bleeding with platelet, plasma, or cryoprecipitate support guided by bleeding/procedure risk rather than fixed lab numbers alone.
Start renal replacement therapy for severe AKI with refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, uremic complications, or fluid overload.
In pregnancy or tetracycline-avoidance contexts, involve infectious diseases/obstetrics early for active non-tetracycline therapy selection.
Report clusters or travel-associated cases according to local public-health requirements and counsel on avoiding chigger habitats, protective clothing, and repellents during future exposure.
